content: Approximately 5% of the global population, equating to 35–40 million individuals worldwide, require prosthetics and orthotics services. The demand for orthotic treatment is at least two to four times higher than that for prosthetic treatment. This need is expected to increase significantly in the coming decades due to the growth in both the global population and life expectancy. As a larger proportion of the aging population will experience disabilities, the demand for these services will rise proportionally. The prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions and noncommunicable diseases, such as diabetes and stroke, is increasing globally. These conditions, if trends persist, will substantially contribute to the growing need for prosthetics and orthotics services. By the mid-21st century, it is estimated that nearly 1% of the global population will require these services. In 2015, an estimated 415 million people were living with diabetes, a number projected to rise to 642 million by 2040. Among individuals with diabetes, 60–70% experience loss of sensation in their feet, putting them at risk of injury. Additionally, 12–15% of people with diabetes develop foot ulcers, which increase the risk of infection, amputation, or even premature death. Proper foot care and the use of orthoses, including appropriate footwear, can reduce these risks, improve healing rates, and prevent amputations. Access to prosthetics and orthotics services is severely limited in many countries. Data on the needs and unmet needs for these services are lacking, and facilities are often concentrated in capital cities or large urban areas. In many countries, only 5–15% of individuals who could benefit from assistive products, including prostheses and orthoses, have access to them. Even in high-income countries, access to these services remains a challenge for many individuals. Governments and stakeholders must collect data on these needs to develop nationwide services and monitor progress toward achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Prosthetics and orthotics services provide significant benefits at multiple levels. They enhance the mobility and functionality of individuals with physical impairments, enabling them to lead active, productive, and independent lives. These services also facilitate access to education and employment, helping to integrate individuals with disabilities into society and providing them with equal opportunities. Economically, these services reduce healthcare costs by accelerating recovery, shortening hospital stays, and decreasing the need for frequent medical interventions. They also contribute to economic growth by enabling a more productive workforce and creating job opportunities in the production and delivery of prosthetic and orthotic components. Access to prosthetics and orthotics services is a fundamental human right. The CRPD obligates states to ensure the availability of high-quality, affordable assistive devices and technologies, including prostheses and orthoses. More than 170 countries have ratified the CRPD, committing to provide these services to those in need. These services are essential for achieving SDG 3, which aims to ensure good health and well-being for all, as well as other SDGs related to education, employment, poverty reduction, and social inclusion. Despite their importance, the development of prosthetics and orthotics services faces numerous challenges. These include the absence of national policies and plans, limited funding, lack of awareness about the benefits of these services, and insufficient data on needs. The availability of appropriate products is limited in many countries, and high-quality devices are often unaffordable. There is also a shortage of qualified personnel, with most professionals concentrated in urban areas, leaving rural populations underserved. Governments must take a leading role in developing and coordinating national prosthetics and orthotics services. This includes involving all relevant stakeholders, such as service users, caregivers, and user groups, in policy development, planning, and monitoring. Establishing a national committee for prosthetics and orthotics can strengthen collaboration and coordination, ensuring countrywide access to these services. A guiding framework, including legislation, policies, strategic plans, and standards, is essential for the development and regulation of prosthetics and orthotics services. Monitoring the implementation of these services is crucial to ensure they meet national goals and regulations. This requires measurable goals, benchmarks, and systematic data collection. International coordination and cooperation are also vital, particularly for countries lacking the capacity, resources, and expertise to develop these services independently.
